## Expo

#### A project for Spain

Registered by the 93rd General Assembly of the BIE on 15 June 1983, Expo 1992 was organised to present the new positioning of Spain. As soon as Juan Carlos I ascended the throne after General Franco's death, he announced the country would host a World Expo. Sixteen years later, with Expo in Seville, the country was able to exhibit its cultural diversity through the pavilions of the Autonomous Regions and to ensure its position in Europe and on the international stage, in part thanks to the presence of the European Community Pavilion located on the "Avenue of Europe".

[![Image 24](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/timeline/World_Expos/1992seville2.jpg)](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/timeline/World_Expos/1992seville2.jpg)

#### A reflection of History

The Expo was prepared for the most part during the Cold War, but its opening took place after it ended, which had important consequences on the organization of the event. Following the fall of the Berlin wall and the reunification of Germany, there were no longer two but one pavilion to represent the country. Georg Lippsmeier's pavilion designed for the Federal Republic of Germany was chosen for this purpose. The USSR pavilion became the Russian Pavilion, while Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia presented themselves as newly independant countries under the common roof of the Baltic countries pavilion. The Expo was also impacted by other historical events such as the Gulf War that impeded Iraq from participating.

#### The Cartuja Island

The theme of the Expo was "The Age of discovery" to celebrate the 500th anniversary of the discovery of the Americas by Christopher Columbus. The Isla de la Cartuja, where the explorer is said to have lived before his journey, was chosen to host the Expo.

#### The Road of the Discoveries

The historical Puerto de las Indias, entryway to the Expo site and the monastery of La Cartuja were both included in the event along the main avenue of the Expo: the Road of the Discoveries. The avenue was composed of 10 thematic pavilions that embarked visitors on a journey through time where they could witness the evolution of science, technology and culture over 500 years. Among other attractions, they were able to board a XVth century caravel before hopping on a spaceship.

#### A rich cultural program

Expo 92 offered many activities, day and night. The site vibrated with the festive Andalusian spirit. Every evening, fireworks and light shows over the Lake of Spain launched the beginning of "Expo-night". The cultural choice was impressive and diverse: visitors could enjoy traditional operas (New York Metropolitan Opera, the Vienna Opera, La Scala of Milan), philharmonic and symphonic orchestras (Celibidache, Abbado, Metha), plays (Laurie Anderson, Centro Dramatico Nacional, Floats), Jazz Festivals and Flamenco or Salsa music until 4 am.

#### Urban development of Seville

The city of Seville benefited greatly from the works done to ensure a high-quality Expo. The airport built a new terminal; a more functional train station replaced the two stations of the city; a new high-speed line was created to link Seville to Madrid; highways were built and the Barqueta, Alamillo, Cartuja and El Cachorro bridges were erected to facilitate the access to the Expo site.

The Expo had a very positive impact on the image of Andalusia as it allowed the region to showcase its organisational and logistical skills.

#### The transformation of the Site

The Cartuja Island, once the Expo ended, became Cartuja 93, a technical and economic development center. Several pavilions were kept, such as the Puerto Rican pavilion, and turned into offices. Additionally, an amusement park was created near the Lake of Spain.

## Mascot

[![Image 25](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/mascots/Mascots_Seville_1992.png)](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/mascots/Mascots_Seville_1992.png)

Curro, the mascot of World Expo 1992, was designed by Heinz Edelman and chosen from 23 designs coming from 15 different countries. His name, Curro, comes from the nickname given in Andalusia to those named Francisco.

A predominantly white bird with the legs of an elephant, Curro’s crest and beak are multi-coloured. Each of the five colours represents a different continent. Curro is a cheerful, curious and affectionate character with plenty of energy. Today, more than 25 years after the Expo, Curro remains in the memories and hearts of all visitors to the Expo.

## Expo

#### A project for Spain

Registered by the 93rd General Assembly of the BIE on 15 June 1983, Expo 1992 was organised to present the new positioning of Spain. As soon as Juan Carlos I ascended the throne after General Franco's death, he announced the country would host a World Expo. Sixteen years later, with Expo in Seville, the country was able to exhibit its cultural diversity through the pavilions of the Autonomous Regions and to ensure its position in Europe and on the international stage, in part thanks to the presence of the European Community Pavilion located on the "Avenue of Europe".

[![Image 24](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/timeline/World_Expos/1992seville2.jpg)](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/timeline/World_Expos/1992seville2.jpg)

#### A reflection of History

The Expo was prepared for the most part during the Cold War, but its opening took place after it ended, which had important consequences on the organization of the event. Following the fall of the Berlin wall and the reunification of Germany, there were no longer two but one pavilion to represent the country. Georg Lippsmeier's pavilion designed for the Federal Republic of Germany was chosen for this purpose. The USSR pavilion became the Russian Pavilion, while Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia presented themselves as newly independant countries under the common roof of the Baltic countries pavilion. The Expo was also impacted by other historical events such as the Gulf War that impeded Iraq from participating.

#### The Cartuja Island

The theme of the Expo was "The Age of discovery" to celebrate the 500th anniversary of the discovery of the Americas by Christopher Columbus. The Isla de la Cartuja, where the explorer is said to have lived before his journey, was chosen to host the Expo.

#### The Road of the Discoveries

The historical Puerto de las Indias, entryway to the Expo site and the monastery of La Cartuja were both included in the event along the main avenue of the Expo: the Road of the Discoveries. The avenue was composed of 10 thematic pavilions that embarked visitors on a journey through time where they could witness the evolution of science, technology and culture over 500 years. Among other attractions, they were able to board a XVth century caravel before hopping on a spaceship.

#### A rich cultural program

Expo 92 offered many activities, day and night. The site vibrated with the festive Andalusian spirit. Every evening, fireworks and light shows over the Lake of Spain launched the beginning of "Expo-night". The cultural choice was impressive and diverse: visitors could enjoy traditional operas (New York Metropolitan Opera, the Vienna Opera, La Scala of Milan), philharmonic and symphonic orchestras (Celibidache, Abbado, Metha), plays (Laurie Anderson, Centro Dramatico Nacional, Floats), Jazz Festivals and Flamenco or Salsa music until 4 am.

#### Urban development of Seville

The city of Seville benefited greatly from the works done to ensure a high-quality Expo. The airport built a new terminal; a more functional train station replaced the two stations of the city; a new high-speed line was created to link Seville to Madrid; highways were built and the Barqueta, Alamillo, Cartuja and El Cachorro bridges were erected to facilitate the access to the Expo site.

The Expo had a very positive impact on the image of Andalusia as it allowed the region to showcase its organisational and logistical skills.

#### The transformation of the Site

The Cartuja Island, once the Expo ended, became Cartuja 93, a technical and economic development center. Several pavilions were kept, such as the Puerto Rican pavilion, and turned into offices. Additionally, an amusement park was created near the Lake of Spain.

## Mascot

[![Image 25](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/mascots/Mascots_Seville_1992.png)](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/mascots/Mascots_Seville_1992.png)

Curro, the mascot of World Expo 1992, was designed by Heinz Edelman and chosen from 23 designs coming from 15 different countries. His name, Curro, comes from the nickname given in Andalusia to those named Francisco.

A predominantly white bird with the legs of an elephant, Curro’s crest and beak are multi-coloured. Each of the five colours represents a different continent. Curro is a cheerful, curious and affectionate character with plenty of energy. Today, more than 25 years after the Expo, Curro remains in the memories and hearts of all visitors to the Expo.

## Expo

Following in the footsteps of Expo 1888, the International Exhibition of Barcelona 1929 was the second World Expo to be held in the city. The Expo, which had ‘Industry, Art and Sport’ as its theme, attracted almost 5.8 million visitors and thoroughly revitalised the modern spirit of the regional capital. A total of 29 nations participated in the Expo, while there were also private (non-official) participants from other countries including the United States and Japan.

Plans for holding a second International Exhibition in Barcelona originated as early as 1905, when Catalan architect and political activist Josep Puig i Cadafalch published an article in ‘La Veu de Catalunya’, demanding a new wave of modernisation for the city. Inspired by the 1888 Exhibition, he called for Barcelona to host another World Expo.

Show More

[![Image 19](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/timeline/World_Expos/Historical/1929barcelona.jpg)](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/timeline/World_Expos/Historical/1929barcelona.jpg)

#### Barcelona: a Modern Metropolis

By the official inauguration of the Expo on 19 May, the city of Barcelona had been thoroughly modernised and many districts had undergone large-scale renovations. The famous Barri Gòtic (Gothic Quarter) was redeveloped, while Spanish avant-garde artists such as Pablo Gargallo, Josep Clarà, and Josep Llimona completed the Plaça de Catalunya with a collection of statues.

The town of Sarrià, which became Barcelona’s new uptown area in 1921, was connected to the central Eixample neighbourhood via an underground railway.  
Barcelona’s França railway station was re-built for the Expo; its two monumental buildings were designed by the architect Pedro Muguruza and inaugurated by King Alfonso XIII. Additionally, modern tarred roads were laid and lit by modern street lights, and the first metro lines entered into service.

#### The Expo site

One of the greatest challenges in planning the Expo was to find a large enough site – over 100 hectares – to host all of the pavilions and exhibitions spaces. Montjuïc, a park overlooking the city’s harbour, was eventually chosen, with the city of Barcelona gaining control of the site from the military. The park was unusual for an Expo site due to it being on a slope, making Expo 1929 the first of its kind to be held on a non-flat surface.

The initial development of the site started in 1917 and lasted until 1923. Several farms on the site were transformed into gardens by French architect, Jean-Claude Nicolas Forestier. Additionally, the Alfonso XIII and Victoria Eugenia Palaces were built on the Expo grounds according to the designs of Josep Puig i Cadafalch.  
Between 1927 and 1929, the other exhibition buildings and pavilions were constructed or extended, including some by famous architects such as A. Font and E. Saigner. Nicolau M. Rubió designed the hotels located on Plaça Espanya, located in front of the main access to the Expo site. The Poble Espanyol (Spanish Town) was built on Montjuïc as a museum to Spanish architecture, featuring 117 buildings inspired by the country’s regional styles.

The centrepiece of the Expo site and the largest building constructed for the Expo was the Palau Nacional, designed in a Spanish Renaissance style by Eugeonia Cendoya and Enric Catà.

#### Industry, Art and Sport

Expo 1929 attracted 5.8 million visitors from all over the world. Among the most popular features of the exhibition was the ‘Juego de Agua y Luz’ fountain, designed by Carles Buigas. The monumental fountain stood out with its multiple water jets illuminated with changing colours, matching the different figures created by the water.

Culture and leisure played a big part of Expo 1929, with activities including theatre shows, concerts, operas and ballets. The old stone quarries of Montjuïc were used to build a Classical Greek Theatre, while visitors could also enjoy light entertainment in a funfair park.

A number of sporting events were organised as part of the Expo, with the site including tennis courts, a swimming pool and a specially built stadium, which hosted athletic competitions and football games.

#### Legacy

In addition to the improvements to Barcelona’s infrastructure and urban development, several structures were kept at the end of the Expo for recreational and cultural uses. Many of these buildings are magnificent examples of 20th century architectural styles, including classicism, modernism and avant-garde.

The Palau Nacional now hosts the Museo Nacional de Arte de Cataluña (MNAC), and the Montjuic Stadium, built for the Expo’s sports events, was later renovated for the 1992 Olympics.

The Palace of Graphic Arts was later turned into the Catalan Archaeological Museum, while the Palace of Agriculture became the Mercat de les Flors (Flower Market). Additionally, the Feria de Muestra de Barcelona, a major venue for concerts, markets and cultural events, was created from three of the Expo’s pavilions. The Poble Espanyol and the Greek Theatre also still remain and are some of Barcelona’s most popular attractions.

The German Pavilion, designed by architect Mies van der Rohe, was an important architectural feature of the Expo. Built with glass, travertine and different kinds of marble, it was demolished after Expo closed. An early symbol of the Modernist movement, the pavilion received much attention and interpretation by successive generations of architects and was therefore rebuilt between 1983 and 1986 as a tribute to its iconic status.

## Expo

Following in the footsteps of Expo 1888, the International Exhibition of Barcelona 1929 was the second World Expo to be held in the city. The Expo, which had ‘Industry, Art and Sport’ as its theme, attracted almost 5.8 million visitors and thoroughly revitalised the modern spirit of the regional capital. A total of 29 nations participated in the Expo, while there were also private (non-official) participants from other countries including the United States and Japan.

Plans for holding a second International Exhibition in Barcelona originated as early as 1905, when Catalan architect and political activist Josep Puig i Cadafalch published an article in ‘La Veu de Catalunya’, demanding a new wave of modernisation for the city. Inspired by the 1888 Exhibition, he called for Barcelona to host another World Expo.

Show More

[![Image 19](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/timeline/World_Expos/Historical/1929barcelona.jpg)](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/images/timeline/World_Expos/Historical/1929barcelona.jpg)

#### Barcelona: a Modern Metropolis

By the official inauguration of the Expo on 19 May, the city of Barcelona had been thoroughly modernised and many districts had undergone large-scale renovations. The famous Barri Gòtic (Gothic Quarter) was redeveloped, while Spanish avant-garde artists such as Pablo Gargallo, Josep Clarà, and Josep Llimona completed the Plaça de Catalunya with a collection of statues.

The town of Sarrià, which became Barcelona’s new uptown area in 1921, was connected to the central Eixample neighbourhood via an underground railway.  
Barcelona’s França railway station was re-built for the Expo; its two monumental buildings were designed by the architect Pedro Muguruza and inaugurated by King Alfonso XIII. Additionally, modern tarred roads were laid and lit by modern street lights, and the first metro lines entered into service.

#### The Expo site

One of the greatest challenges in planning the Expo was to find a large enough site – over 100 hectares – to host all of the pavilions and exhibitions spaces. Montjuïc, a park overlooking the city’s harbour, was eventually chosen, with the city of Barcelona gaining control of the site from the military. The park was unusual for an Expo site due to it being on a slope, making Expo 1929 the first of its kind to be held on a non-flat surface.

The initial development of the site started in 1917 and lasted until 1923. Several farms on the site were transformed into gardens by French architect, Jean-Claude Nicolas Forestier. Additionally, the Alfonso XIII and Victoria Eugenia Palaces were built on the Expo grounds according to the designs of Josep Puig i Cadafalch.  
Between 1927 and 1929, the other exhibition buildings and pavilions were constructed or extended, including some by famous architects such as A. Font and E. Saigner. Nicolau M. Rubió designed the hotels located on Plaça Espanya, located in front of the main access to the Expo site. The Poble Espanyol (Spanish Town) was built on Montjuïc as a museum to Spanish architecture, featuring 117 buildings inspired by the country’s regional styles.

The centrepiece of the Expo site and the largest building constructed for the Expo was the Palau Nacional, designed in a Spanish Renaissance style by Eugeonia Cendoya and Enric Catà.

#### Industry, Art and Sport

Expo 1929 attracted 5.8 million visitors from all over the world. Among the most popular features of the exhibition was the ‘Juego de Agua y Luz’ fountain, designed by Carles Buigas. The monumental fountain stood out with its multiple water jets illuminated with changing colours, matching the different figures created by the water.

Culture and leisure played a big part of Expo 1929, with activities including theatre shows, concerts, operas and ballets. The old stone quarries of Montjuïc were used to build a Classical Greek Theatre, while visitors could also enjoy light entertainment in a funfair park.

A number of sporting events were organised as part of the Expo, with the site including tennis courts, a swimming pool and a specially built stadium, which hosted athletic competitions and football games.

#### Legacy

In addition to the improvements to Barcelona’s infrastructure and urban development, several structures were kept at the end of the Expo for recreational and cultural uses. Many of these buildings are magnificent examples of 20th century architectural styles, including classicism, modernism and avant-garde.

The Palau Nacional now hosts the Museo Nacional de Arte de Cataluña (MNAC), and the Montjuic Stadium, built for the Expo’s sports events, was later renovated for the 1992 Olympics.

The Palace of Graphic Arts was later turned into the Catalan Archaeological Museum, while the Palace of Agriculture became the Mercat de les Flors (Flower Market). Additionally, the Feria de Muestra de Barcelona, a major venue for concerts, markets and cultural events, was created from three of the Expo’s pavilions. The Poble Espanyol and the Greek Theatre also still remain and are some of Barcelona’s most popular attractions.

The German Pavilion, designed by architect Mies van der Rohe, was an important architectural feature of the Expo. Built with glass, travertine and different kinds of marble, it was demolished after Expo closed. An early symbol of the Modernist movement, the pavilion received much attention and interpretation by successive generations of architects and was therefore rebuilt between 1983 and 1986 as a tribute to its iconic status.

**Seville** ([/s ə ˈ v ɪ l/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_sə-VIL_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): _Sevilla_, pronounced[[seˈβiʎa]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/b/b9/Pronunciation_of_Seville_in_Spanish.ogg/Pronunciation_of_Seville_in_Spanish.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pronunciation_of_Seville_in_Spanish.ogg "File:Pronunciation of Seville in Spanish.ogg")locally[[seˈβiʝa]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is the capital and largest city of the [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain")[autonomous community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_communities_of_Spain "Autonomous communities of Spain") of [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia") and the [province of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Seville "Province of Seville"). It is situated on the lower reaches of the [River Guadalquivir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalquivir "Guadalquivir"), in the southwest of the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula").

Seville has a municipal population of about 686,742 as of 2024,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-population-1) and a [metropolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_metropolitan_area "Seville metropolitan area") population of about 1.5 million, making it the largest city in Andalusia and the [5th-largest city in Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranked_lists_of_Spanish_municipalities#By_population "Ranked lists of Spanish municipalities"). Its [old town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_town "Old town"), with an area of 4 square kilometres (2 sq mi), contains a [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")[World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") comprising three buildings: the [Alcázar palace complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville "Alcázar of Seville"), the [Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral "Seville Cathedral") and the [General Archive of the Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Archive_of_the_Indies "General Archive of the Indies"). The [Port of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Seville "Port of Seville"), located about 80 kilometres (50 miles) from the Atlantic Ocean, is the only river harbour in Spain.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-ESA2020-5) The capital of Andalusia experiences hot temperatures in the summer, with daily maximums routinely above 35°C (95°F) in July and August.

Seville was founded as the [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") city of _Hispalis_. Known as _Ishbiliyah_ after the [Islamic conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_conquest_of_Hispania "Umayyad conquest of Hispania") in 711, Seville became the centre of the independent [Taifa of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Seville "Taifa of Seville") following the collapse of the [Caliphate of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Caliphate of Córdoba") in the early 11th century; later it was ruled by [Almoravids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravids "Almoravids") and [Almohads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohad_dynasty "Almohad dynasty") until being incorporated into the [Crown of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile "Crown of Castile") in 1248.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Christian-Muslim_Relations._A_Bibliographical_History._Volume_4_(1200%E2%80%931350)-6) Owing to its role as the gateway of the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire")'s trans-atlantic trade, managed from the [Casa de Contratación](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Contrataci%C3%B3n "Casa de Contratación"), Seville became one of the largest cities in [Western Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe") in the 16th century. Following a deterioration in drought conditions in the Guadalquivir, the American trade gradually moved away from the city of Seville, in favour initially of downstream-dependent berths and eventually of the [Bay of Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_C%C3%A1diz "Bay of Cádiz") – to which were eventually transferred control of both the [fleets of the Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_treasure_fleet "Spanish treasure fleet") (1680) and the [Casa de Contratación](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Contrataci%C3%B3n "Casa de Contratación") (1717).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-7):430–431

The 20th century in Seville saw the tribulations of the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War"), decisive cultural milestones such as the [Ibero-American Exposition of 1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibero-American_Exposition_of_1929 "Ibero-American Exposition of 1929") and [Expo '92](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Expo_'92 "Seville Expo '92"), and the city's election as the capital of the [Autonomous Community of Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusian_Autonomous_Government "Andalusian Autonomous Government").

## Name

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Name")]

### Etymology and derivatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Etymology and derivatives")]

According to Manuel Pellicer Catalán, the name "Sevilla" derives from the ancient name _Spal_, meaning "lowland" in the [Phoenician language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_language "Phoenician language") ([cognate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognate "Cognate") to the Hebrew _[Shfela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shfela "Shfela")_ שְּׁפֵלָה and the Arabic _Asfal_ أسفل).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-SPAL:_Revista_de_prehistoria_y_arqueolog%C3%ADa_de_la_Universidad_de_Sevilla-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-9) It is ultimately from Phoenician _sefela_, meaning "plain, valley".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-10)_Hisbaal_ is another old name for Seville. It appears to have originated during the [Phoenician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia") colonisation of the [Tartessian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartessos "Tartessos") culture in south-western Iberia, and according to a new proposal, it refers to the god [Baal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baal "Baal").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-11)

During [Roman rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania "Hispania"), the name was Latinised as _Hispal_ and later as _Hispalis_. After the [Umayyad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad "Umayyad") invasion, this name remained in use among the [Mozarabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozarabs "Mozarabs"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Mena_1992-12) being adapted into Arabic as _Išbīliya_ (إشبيلية): since the /p/ [phoneme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoneme "Phoneme") does not exist in Arabic, it was replaced by /b/; the Latin place-name suffix _-is_ was Arabized as _-iya_, and _a_/æ/ turned into _ī_/iː/ due to the phonetic phenomenon called _[imāla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Im%C4%81la "Imāla")_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-13)

In the meantime, the city's official name had been changed to _Ḥimṣ al-Andalus_ (حمص الأندلس), in reference to the city of [Homs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homs "Homs") in modern Syria, [the jund of which](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jund_Hims "Jund Hims") Seville had been assigned to upon the Umayyad conquest;[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-15)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Mena_1992-12)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-16) "Ḥimṣ al-Andalus" remained a customary and affectionate name for the city during the whole period throughout the Muslim Arab world,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Mena_1992-12)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-18) being referred to for example in the encyclopedia of [Yaqut al-Hamawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaqut_al-Hamawi "Yaqut al-Hamawi")[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-19) or in [Abu al-Baqa ar-Rundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_al-Baqa_ar-Rundi "Abu al-Baqa ar-Rundi")'s _[Ritha' al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritha'\_al-Andalus "Ritha' al-Andalus")_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-20)

### Motto

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Motto")]

Main article: [NO8DO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NO8DO "NO8DO")

_NO8DO_ is the official motto of Seville, popularly believed to be a [rebus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebus "Rebus") signifying the Spanish _No me ha dejado_, meaning "She [Seville] has not abandoned me". The phrase, pronounced with [synalepha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synalepha "Synalepha") as [[no ma ðeˈxaðo]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish") (no-madeja-do), is written with an eight in the middle representing the word _madeja_[[maˈðexa]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish") "skein [of wool]". Legend states that the title was given by King [Alfonso X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile "Alfonso X of Castile"), who was resident in the city's [Alcázar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville "Alcázar of Seville") and supported by the citizens when his son, later [Sancho IV of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sancho_IV_of_Castile "Sancho IV of Castile"), tried to usurp the throne from him.

The emblem is present on Seville's municipal flag, and features on city property such as manhole covers, and [Christopher Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Columbus "Christopher Columbus")'s tomb in the cathedral.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: History")]

Main articles: [History of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Seville "History of Seville") and [Timeline of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Seville "Timeline of Seville")

Seville is approximately 2,200 years old. The passage of the various civilizations instrumental in its growth has left the city with a distinct personality, and a large and well-preserved historical centre.

### Early periods

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Early periods")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Tesoro_del_Carambolo_-_Museo_Arqueol%C3%B3gico_de_Sevilla.jpg/250px-Tesoro_del_Carambolo_-_Museo_Arqueol%C3%B3gico_de_Sevilla.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tesoro_del_Carambolo_-_Museo_Arqueol%C3%B3gico_de_Sevilla.jpg)

[Treasure of El Carambolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasure_of_El_Carambolo "Treasure of El Carambolo"), belonging to the ancient [Tartessian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartessos "Tartessos") sanctuary located 3 kilometers west of Seville

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Ca%C3%B1os_de_Carmona_en_calle_Luis_Montoto_%282%29.jpg/250px-Ca%C3%B1os_de_Carmona_en_calle_Luis_Montoto_%282%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ca%C3%B1os_de_Carmona_en_calle_Luis_Montoto_(2).jpg)

Section of [Caños de Carmona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ca%C3%B1os_de_Carmona "Caños de Carmona")

The mythological founder of the city is Hercules ([Heracles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heracles "Heracles")), commonly identified with the Phoenician god [Melqart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melqart "Melqart"), who the myth says sailed through the [Strait of Gibraltar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strait_of_Gibraltar "Strait of Gibraltar") to the Atlantic, and founded trading posts at the current sites of [Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz "Cádiz") and of Seville.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-21) The original core of the city, in the neighbourhood of the present-day street, Cuesta del Rosario, dates to the 8th century BC,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Salgueiro2007-22) when Seville was on an island in the [Guadalquivir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalquivir "Guadalquivir").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Mena1985-23) Archaeological excavations in 1999 found anthropic remains under the north wall of the Real Alcázar dating to the 8th–7th century BC.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-24) The town was called _Hisbaal_ by the Phoenicians and by the Tartessians, the indigenous pre-Roman Iberian people of [Tartessos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartessos "Tartessos"), who controlled the Guadalquivir Valley at the time.

The city was known from [Roman times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania "Hispania") as _Hispal_ and later as _Hispalis_. Hispalis developed into one of the great market and industrial centres of Hispania, while the nearby Roman city of [Italica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italica "Italica") (present-day [Santiponce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiponce "Santiponce"), birthplace of the Roman emperors [Trajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan "Trajan") and [Hadrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrian "Hadrian"))[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Nash2005-25) remained a typically Roman residential city. Large-scale Roman archaeological remains can be seen there and at the nearby town of [Carmona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmona,_Spain "Carmona, Spain") as well.

Existing Roman features in Seville itself include the remains exposed _[in situ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_situ "In situ")_ in the underground Antiquarium of the [Metropol Parasol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropol_Parasol "Metropol Parasol") building, the remnants of an [aqueduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ca%C3%B1os_de_Carmona "Caños de Carmona"), three pillars of a [temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_temple "Roman temple") in _Mármoles_ Street, the columns of [La Alameda de Hércules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Alameda,_Seville "La Alameda, Seville") and the remains in the [Patio de Banderas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patio_de_Banderas?action=edit&redlink=1 "Patio de Banderas (page does not exist)") square near the [Seville Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral "Seville Cathedral"). The walls surrounding the city were originally built during the rule of [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar "Julius Caesar"), but their current course and design were the result of Moorish reconstructions.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-degelo.com-26)

Following Roman rule, there were successive conquests of the Roman province of _[Hispania Baetica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania\_Baetica "Hispania Baetica")_ by the Germanic [Vandals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandals "Vandals"), [Suebi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suebi "Suebi") and [Visigoths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigoths "Visigoths") during the 5th and 6th centuries.

### Middle Ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Middle Ages")]

In the wake of the [Islamic conquest of the Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_conquest_of_the_Iberian_Peninsula "Islamic conquest of the Iberian Peninsula"), Seville (_Spalis_) was seemingly taken by [Musa ibn Nusayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_ibn_Nusayr "Musa ibn Nusayr") in the late summer of 712, while he was on his way to [Mérida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9rida,_Spain "Mérida, Spain").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-gathane-27) Yet it had to be retaken in July 713 by troops led by his son [Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Aziz_ibn_Musa "Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa"), as the Visigothic population who had fled to [Beja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beja,_Portugal "Beja, Portugal") had returned to Seville once Musa left for Mérida.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-gathane-27) The seat of the [Wali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wali_(administrative_title) "Wali (administrative title)") of [Al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Andalus "Al-Andalus") (administrative division of the [Umayyad Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate "Umayyad Caliphate")) was thus established in the city until 716,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-gathane-27) when the capital of Al-Andalus was relocated to [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba,_Spain "Córdoba, Spain").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-28)

Seville (_Ishbīliya_) [was sacked by Vikings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_raid_on_Seville "Viking raid on Seville") in the mid-9th century. After Vikings arrived by 25 September 844, Seville fell to invaders on 1 October, and they stood for 40 days before they fled from the city.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-29) During Umayyad rule, under an Andalusi-Arab framework, the bulk of the population were [Muladi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muwallad "Muwallad") converts, to which Christian and Jewish minorities added up.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValencia1994136%E2%80%93137;_138-30) Up until the arrival of the [Almohads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almohads "Almohads") in the 12th century, the city remained as the see of a Metropolitan Archbishop,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-31) the leading Christian religious figure in al-Andalus. However, the transfer of the relics of [Saint Isidore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidore_of_Seville "Isidore of Seville") to [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Spain "León, Spain") circa 1063, in the taifa period, already hinted at a possible worsening of the situation of the local Christian minority.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-32)

A [powerful _taifa_ kingdom with capital in Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Seville "Taifa of Seville") emerged after 1023,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValencia1994139-33) in the wake of the [fitna of al-Andalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitna_of_al-Andalus "Fitna of al-Andalus"). Ruled by the [Abbadid dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbadid_dynasty "Abbadid dynasty"), the taifa grew by aggregation of smaller neighbouring _taifas_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValencia1994139-33) During the taifa period, Seville became an important scholarly and literary centre.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValencia1994139-33) After several months of siege, Seville was conquered by the [Almoravids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravids "Almoravids") in 1091.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-34)

The city fell to the Almohads on 17 January 1147 (12 [Shaʽban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sha%CA%BDban "Shaʽban") 541).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEl_Hour1999289-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-36) After an informal Almohad settlement in Seville during the early stages of the Almohad presence in the Iberian Peninsula and then a brief relocation of the capital of al-Andalus to Córdoba in 1162 (which had dire consequences for Seville, reportedly depopulated and under starvation),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-37) Seville became the definitive seat of the Andalusi part of the Almohad Empire in 1163,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-39) a twin capital alongside [Marrakesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrakesh "Marrakesh"). Almohads carried out a large urban renewal.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-40) By the end of the 12th century, the walled enclosure perhaps contained 80,000 inhabitants.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-41)

See also: [Siege of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Seville "Siege of Seville")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Patio_de_las_doncellas-ret.jpg/330px-Patio_de_las_doncellas-ret.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Patio_de_las_doncellas-ret.jpg)

The _Patio de las Doncellas_ in the [Alcázar of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A1zar_of_Seville "Alcázar of Seville")

In the wider context of the Castilian–Leonese conquest of the Guadalquivir Valley that ensued in the 13th century, [Ferdinand III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_III_of_Castile "Ferdinand III of Castile") laid siege on Seville in 1247. A [naval blockade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_blockade "Naval blockade") came to prevent relief of the city.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-42) The city surrendered on 23 November 1248,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-O'Callaghan1975-43) after fifteen months of siege. The conditions of capitulation contemplated the eviction of the population, with contemporary sources seemingly confirming that a mass movement of people out of Seville indeed took place.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-44)

The city's development continued after the [Castilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile "Crown of Castile") conquest in 1248. Public buildings were constructed including churches—many of which were built in the [Mudéjar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar "Mudéjar") and [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") styles—such as the Seville Cathedral, built during the 15th century with [Gothic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Norwich2001-45) Other Moorish buildings were converted into Catholic edifices, as was customary of the Catholic Church during the _[Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista "Reconquista")_. The Moors' Palace became the Castilian royal residence, and during [Pedro I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile")'s rule it was replaced by the Alcázar (the upper levels are still used by the [Spanish royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_royal_family "Spanish royal family") as the official Seville residence).

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Seville_panorama.jpg/960px-Seville_panorama.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seville_panorama.jpg "Cathedral of Saint Mary from Constitución Avenue")

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seville_panorama.jpg "File:Seville panorama.jpg")

[Cathedral of Saint Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral "Seville Cathedral") from Constitución Avenue

Seville was the starting point of the [1391 anti-Jewish massacres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_1391 "Massacre of 1391"), which soon spread across Castile and Aragon.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-46) In the aftermath, all of Seville's synagogues were seized and converted into churches (renamed Santa María la Blanca, San Bartolomé, Santa Cruz, and Convento Madre de Dios). The Jewish quarter's land and shops (which were located in modern-day [Santa Cruz neighbourhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz,_Seville "Santa Cruz, Seville")) were appropriated by the church and many Jewish homes were burned down. 4,000 Jews were killed during the pogrom and many others were [forced to convert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B'nei_Anusim "B'nei Anusim").

The first tribunal of the [Spanish Inquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Inquisition "Spanish Inquisition") was instituted in Seville in 1478. Its primary charge was to ensure that all nominal Christians were really behaving like Christians, and not practicing what Judaism they could in secret. At first, the activity of the Inquisition was limited to the dioceses of [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Seville "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Seville") and [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Roman Catholic Diocese of Córdoba"), where the Dominican friar, Alonso de Ojeda, had detected [converso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Converso "Converso") activity.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-ojeda-47) The first [Auto de Fé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto-da-f%C3%A9 "Auto-da-fé") took place in Seville on 6 February 1481, when six people were burned alive. Alonso de Ojeda himself gave the sermon. The Inquisition then grew rapidly. The Plaza de San Francisco was the site of the 'autos de fé'. By 1492, tribunals existed in eight Castilian cities: Ávila, Córdoba, Jaén, Medina del Campo, Segovia, Sigüenza, Toledo, and Valladolid;[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-48) and by the [Alhambra Decree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra_Decree "Alhambra Decree") all Jews were [forced to convert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anusim "Anusim") to Catholicism or be exiled (expelled) from Spain.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Levine-49)

### Early modern period

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Early modern period")]

Following the [Columbian exploration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus "Voyages of Christopher Columbus") of the [New World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World "New World"), Seville was chosen as headquarters of the [Casa de Contratación](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Contrataci%C3%B3n "Casa de Contratación") in 1503, which was the decisive development for Seville becoming the port and gateway to the Indies.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-FOOTNOTEP%C3%A9rez-Malla%C3%ADna199715-50) Unlike other harbors, reaching the port of Seville required sailing about 80 kilometres (50 mi) up the River Guadalquivir. The choice of Seville was made in spite of the difficulties for navigation in the Guadalquivir stemming from the increasing [tonnage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonnage "Tonnage") of ships as a result of the relentless drive to make maritime transport cheaper during the late Middle Ages.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-FOOTNOTEP%C3%A9rez-Malla%C3%ADna199716-51) Nevertheless, technical suitability issues notwithstanding, the choice was still reasonable in the sense that Seville had become the largest demographic, economic and financial centre of Christian Andalusia in the late Middle Ages.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-52) In addition, factors favouring the choice of Seville include the Andalusian coastline being largely under the seigneurial control of the [House of Medina Sidonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Medina_Sidonia "House of Medina Sidonia"), Seville enjoying an important hinterland and administrative expertise, and its inland location also providing conditions for military security and enforcement of tax control.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPacheco_Morales-Padr%C3%B3n2021408%E2%80%93409-53)

A 'golden age of development' commenced in Seville, due to its being the only port awarded the royal monopoly for trade with [Spanish Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas "Spanish colonization of the Americas") and the influx of riches from them. Since only [sailing ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winds_in_the_Age_of_Sail "Winds in the Age of Sail") leaving from and returning to the inland port of Seville could engage in trade with the Spanish Americas, merchants from Europe and other trade centers needed to be in Seville to acquire New World trade goods. The city's population grew to more than a hundred thousand people.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-54)

Seville in the late 16th century, [Museum of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_America "Museum of America"), Madrid

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Gran_peste_de_Sevilla.jpg/250px-Gran_peste_de_Sevilla.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gran_peste_de_Sevilla.jpg)

Anonymous painting illustrating the effects of the 1649 plague

In the early 17th c., Seville's monopoly on overseas trade was broken, with the port of [Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz "Cádiz") now the monopoly port of trade as [silting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siltation "Siltation") of the Guadalquivir river in the 1620s made Seville's harbors harder to use.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Nash-2005-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-56) The [Great Plague of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_Seville "Great Plague of Seville") in 1649, exacerbated by excessive flooding of the Guadalquivir, reduced the population by almost half, and it did not recover until the early 19th century.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-58) By the 18th century, Seville's international importance was in steep decline, after the monopoly port for the trade to the Americas was relocated to Cádiz. Cádiz had gifted the Bourbon claimant to the throne in the [War of the Spanish Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Spanish_Succession "War of the Spanish Succession") funding that helped it pursue the war. The reward to Cádiz was the rights of the monopoly port. The [House of Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Contrataci%C3%B3n "Casa de Contratación") (which registered ships, cargoes, and persons travelling to the New World), and the large scale overseas commercial enterprises of the [merchant guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consulado_de_mercaders?action=edit&redlink=1 "Consulado de mercaders (page does not exist)") relocated to Cádiz. The House of Trade had been housed in rented quarters, but the purpose-built headquarters of the merchant guild was left vacant.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-59)

During the monarchy of [Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain"), the [Archive of the Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archive_of_the_Indies "Archive of the Indies") was established in Seville in the old headquarters of the merchant guild. Documents pertaining to Spain's overseas empire were moved there from existing archival repositories, including [Simancas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simancas "Simancas") and the House of Trade, were consolidated in a single repository. One scholar argues that the establishment of the [Archive of the Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Archive_of_the_Indies "General Archive of the Indies") marks a decisive moment in Spain's history, with the 18th c. Bourbon monarchy conceiving of its overseas territories as colonies of the metropole rather than entities under the jurisdiction of the crown on an equal basis as the kingdoms in the Iberian peninsula.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-60)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Domingo_Mart%C3%ADnez%2C_Real_m%C3%A1scara_de_la_f%C3%A1brica_de_tabacos.jpg/250px-Domingo_Mart%C3%ADnez%2C_Real_m%C3%A1scara_de_la_f%C3%A1brica_de_tabacos.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Domingo_Mart%C3%ADnez,_Real_m%C3%A1scara_de_la_f%C3%A1brica_de_tabacos.jpg)

1747 parade organized by the workers of the [Royal Tobacco Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Tobacco_Factory "Royal Tobacco Factory")

During the 18th century Charles III promoted Seville's industries. Construction of the [_Real Fábrica de Tabacos_ (Royal Tobacco Factory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Tobacco_Factory "Royal Tobacco Factory") began in 1728. It was the second-largest building in Spain, after the royal residence [El Escorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Escorial "El Escorial").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Since the 1950s it has been the seat of the rectorate (administration) of the [University of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Seville "University of Seville"), as well as its Schools of Law, Philology (language/letters), Geography, and History.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-61)

More operas have been set in Seville than in any other city of Europe. In 2012, a study of experts concluded the total number of operas set in Seville is 153. Among the composers who fell in love with the city are [Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beethoven "Beethoven") (_[Fidelio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidelio "Fidelio")_), [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozart "Mozart") (_[The Marriage of Figaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Marriage\_of\_Figaro "The Marriage of Figaro")_ and _[Don Giovanni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don\_Giovanni "Don Giovanni")_), [Rossini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rossini "Rossini") (_[The Barber of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Barber\_of\_Seville "The Barber of Seville")_), [Donizetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donizetti "Donizetti") (_[La favorite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_favorite "La favorite")_), and [Bizet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bizet "Bizet") (_[Carmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen "Carmen")_).[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-62)

The first newspaper in Spain outside of Madrid was Seville's _Hebdomario útil de Seville_, which began publication in 1758.

### Late modern history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Late modern history")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Muelle_y_Torre_del_Oro_Sevilla%2C_RP-F-F01139-CY.jpg/330px-Muelle_y_Torre_del_Oro_Sevilla%2C_RP-F-F01139-CY.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Muelle_y_Torre_del_Oro_Sevilla,_RP-F-F01139-CY.jpg)

The Torre del Oro and the harbor in the second half of the 19th century

Between 1825 and 1833, [Melchor Cano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melchor_Cano "Melchor Cano") acted as chief architect in Seville; most of the urban planning policy and architectural modifications of the city were made by him and his collaborator Jose Manuel Arjona y Cuba.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-63)

Industrial architecture surviving today from the first half of the 19th century includes the ceramics factory installed in the [Carthusian monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Carthusian_monasteries "List of Carthusian monasteries") at [La Cartuja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isla_de_La_Cartuja "Isla de La Cartuja") in 1841 by the Pickman family, and now home to the El Centro Andaluz de Arte Contemporáneo (CAAC),[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-al-64) which manages the collections of the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Sevilla.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-NavarroTorres2002-65) It also houses the rectory of the UNIA.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-66)

In the years that Queen [Isabel II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_II_of_Spain "Isabella II of Spain") ruled directly, about 1843–1868, the Sevillian bourgeoisie invested in a construction boom unmatched in the city's history. The [Isabel II bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puente_de_Isabel_II "Puente de Isabel II"), better known as the Triana bridge, dates from this period; street lighting was expanded in the municipality and most of the streets were paved during this time as well.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-A-67)

By the second half of the 19th century, Seville had begun an expansion supported by railway construction and the demolition of part of its ancient walls, allowing the urban space of the city to grow eastward and southward. The _Sevillana de Electricidad_ Company was created in 1894 to provide electric power throughout the municipality,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-68) and in 1901 the _Plaza de Armas_ railway station was inaugurated.

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Expo_sevilla_1929_poster.jpg/250px-Expo_sevilla_1929_poster.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Expo_sevilla_1929_poster.jpg)

Poster for the [Ibero-American Exposition of 1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibero-American_Exposition_of_1929 "Ibero-American Exposition of 1929")

The [Museum of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Fine_Arts_of_Seville "Museum of Fine Arts of Seville") (_Museo de Bellas Artes de Sevilla_) opened in 1904.

In 1929 the city hosted the [Ibero-American Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibero-American_Exposition_of_1929 "Ibero-American Exposition of 1929"), which accelerated the southern expansion of the city and created new public spaces such as the _[Parque de María Luisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque\_de\_Mar%C3%ADa\_Luisa "Parque de María Luisa")_ (Maria Luisa Park) and the adjoining [_Plaza de España_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_de_Espa%C3%B1a,_Seville "Plaza de España, Seville"). Not long before the opening, the Spanish government began a modernisation of the city in order to prepare for the expected crowds by erecting new hotels and widening the mediaeval streets to allow for the movement of automobiles.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Luce1929-69)

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/EL_GRAL._VARELA_EN_UN_DISCURSO_EN_UN_BALC%C3%93N._AUTOR-_AN%C3%93NIMO.jpg/250px-EL_GRAL._VARELA_EN_UN_DISCURSO_EN_UN_BALC%C3%93N._AUTOR-_AN%C3%93NIMO.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EL_GRAL._VARELA_EN_UN_DISCURSO_EN_UN_BALC%C3%93N._AUTOR-_AN%C3%93NIMO.jpg)

[General Varela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Enrique_Varela "José Enrique Varela") rallying military and civilians in Seville (September 1936)

Seville fell very quickly at the beginning of the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War") in 1936. General [Queipo de Llano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queipo_de_Llano "Queipo de Llano") carried out a coup within the city, quickly capturing the city centre.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Thomas-70) Radio Seville opposed the uprising and called for the peasants to come to the city for arms, while workers' groups established barricades.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Thomas-70) Queipo then moved to capture Radio Seville, which he used to broadcast propaganda on behalf of the Francoist forces.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Thomas-70) After the initial takeover of the city, resistance continued among residents of the working-class neighbourhoods for some time, until a series of fierce reprisals took place.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-71)

Under [Francisco Franco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Franco "Francisco Franco")'s rule Spain was officially neutral in World War II (although it did collaborate with the [Axis powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers")),[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Payne2008-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Bowen2006-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-Corporation2004-74) and like the rest of the country, Seville remained largely economically and culturally isolated from the outside world. In 1953 the shipyard of Seville was opened, eventually employing more than 2,000 workers in the 1970s. Before the existence of wetlands regulation in the Guadalquivir basin, Seville suffered regular heavy flooding; perhaps worst of all were the floods that occurred in November 1961 when the River Tamarguillo, a tributary of the Guadalquivir, overflowed as a result of a prodigious downpour of rain, and Seville was consequently declared a disaster zone.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-PfisterBr%C3%A1zdil2013-75)

Trade unionism in Seville began during the 1960s with the underground organisational activities of the Workers' Commissions or Comisiones Obreras (CCOO), in factories such as Hytasa, the Astilleros shipyards, Hispano Aviación, etc. Several of the movement's leaders were arrested in 1972, and later sentenced to prison in 1973.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-77)

### Recent developments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Recent developments")]

On 3 April 1979 Spain held its first democratic municipal elections after the end of Franco's dictatorship; councillors representing four different political parties were elected in Seville. On 5 November 1982, [Pope John Paul II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_Paul_II "Pope John Paul II") arrived in Seville to officiate at a Mass before more than half a million people at the fairgrounds. He visited the city again on 13 June 1993, for the International Eucharistic Congress.

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Expo_Sevilla002.jpg/250px-Expo_Sevilla002.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Expo_Sevilla002.jpg)

European Union pavilion of the [1992 Universal Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Expo_'92 "Seville Expo '92") as it was at the time

In 1992, coinciding with the fifth centenary of the [Discovery of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus "Voyages of Christopher Columbus"), the [Universal Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Expo_'92 "Seville Expo '92") was held for six months in Seville, on the occasion of which the local communications network and urban infrastructure was greatly improved under a 1987 [PGOU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGOU "PGOU") plan launched by Mayor [Manuel del Valle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_del_Valle "Manuel del Valle"):[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-abc-78) the SE-30 ring road around the city was completed and new highways were constructed; the new [Seville-Santa Justa railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville-Santa_Justa_railway_station "Seville-Santa Justa railway station") had opened in 1991, while the Spanish High-Speed Rail system, the _[Alta Velocidad Española](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alta\_Velocidad\_Espa%C3%B1ola "Alta Velocidad Española")_ (AVE), began to operate between Madrid-Seville. The [Seville Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Airport "Seville Airport") was expanded with a new terminal building designed by the architect [Rafael Moneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Moneo "Rafael Moneo"), and various other improvements were made. The [Alamillo Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puente_del_Alamillo "Puente del Alamillo") and the [Centenario Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centenario_Bridge "Centenario Bridge"), both crossing over the Guadalquivir, also were built for the occasion. Some of the installations remaining at the site after the exposition were converted into the Scientific and Technological Park [Cartuja 93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartuja_93 "Cartuja 93").

In 2004 the Metropol Parasol project, commonly known as _Las Setas_ ('The Mushrooms'), due to the appearance of the structure, was launched to revitalise the _Plaza de la Encarnación_, for years used as a car park and seen as a dead spot between more popular tourist destinations in the city. The Metropol Parasol was completed in March 2011,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-79) costing just over €102 million in total, more than twice as much as originally planned.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-80) Constructed from crossed wooden beams, _Las Setas_ is said to be the largest timber-framed structure in the world.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-81)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/%28Sevilla%29_Seville%2C_Spain_%2849104522676%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-%28Sevilla%29_Seville%2C_Spain_%2849104522676%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:(Sevilla)_Seville,_Spain_(49104522676)_(cropped).jpg)

Satellite imagery of Seville ([Sentinel-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentinel-2 "Sentinel-2"), [Copernicus Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copernicus_Programme "Copernicus Programme"), [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency"))

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/MTN50-0984-2006-cns-Sevilla.jpg/500px-MTN50-0984-2006-cns-Sevilla.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MTN50-0984-2006-cns-Sevilla.jpg)

Seville sheet of MTN50 (Spain's National Topographic Map at 1:50,000 scale), at its first digital edition (year 2006)

Seville has an area of 141 km 2 (54 sq mi), according to the National Topographic Map (_Mapa Topográfico Nacional_) series from the _Instituto Geográfico Nacional–Centro Nacional de Información Geográfica_, the country's civilian survey organisation (pages 984, 985 and 1002). The city is situated in the fertile valley of the River Guadalquivir. The average height [above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level") is 7 metres (23 feet). Most of the city is on the east side of the river, while [Triana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triana,_Seville "Triana, Seville"), [La Cartuja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Cartuja,_Seville "La Cartuja, Seville") and [Los Remedios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Remedios,_Seville "Los Remedios, Seville") are on the west side. The [Aljarafe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albaida_del_Aljarafe "Albaida del Aljarafe") region lies further west, and is considered part of the [metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_metropolitan_area "Seville metropolitan area"). The city has boundaries on the north with [La Rinconada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Rinconada,_Andalusia "La Rinconada, Andalusia"), [La Algaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Algaba "La Algaba") and [Santiponce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiponce "Santiponce"); on the east with [Alcalá de Guadaira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcal%C3%A1_de_Guadaira "Alcalá de Guadaira"); on the south with [Dos Hermanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dos_Hermanas "Dos Hermanas") and [Gelves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelves "Gelves") and on the west with [San Juan de Aznalfarache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan_de_Aznalfarache "San Juan de Aznalfarache"), [Tomares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomares "Tomares") and [Camas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camas,_Seville "Camas, Seville").

Seville is on the same [parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/37th_parallel_north "37th parallel north") as United States west coast city [San Jose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose,_California "San Jose, California") in central California. [São Miguel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Miguel_Island "São Miguel Island"), the main island of the [Azores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores "Azores") archipelago, lies on the same latitude. Further east from Seville in the [Mediterranean Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Basin "Mediterranean Basin"), it is on the same latitude as [Catania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catania "Catania") in Sicily, Italy and just south of [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens"), the capital of [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"). Beyond that, it is located on the same parallel as South Korean capital, [Seoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul "Seoul"). Seville is located inland, not very far from the Andalusian coast, but still sees a much more continental climate than the nearest port cities, [Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz "Cádiz") and [Huelva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huelva "Huelva"). Its distance from the sea makes summers in Sevilla much hotter than along the coastline.

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Climate")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Toits_Guadalquivir_ponts_S%C3%A9ville_Espagne.jpg/250px-Toits_Guadalquivir_ponts_S%C3%A9ville_Espagne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Toits_Guadalquivir_ponts_S%C3%A9ville_Espagne.jpg)

Skyline of Seville from the top of the [Giralda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giralda "Giralda")

Seville's climate is a [hot-summer Mediterranean climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot-summer_Mediterranean_climate "Hot-summer Mediterranean climate") ([Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")_Csa_), featuring very hot, long, dry summers and mild winters with moderate rainfall.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-82) Seville has an annual average temperature of 19.6°C (67°F). The annual average temperature is 25.7°C (78°F) during the day and 13.3°C (56°F) at night.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-83) Seville is located in the [Guadalquivir Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baetic_Depression "Baetic Depression"), which is often referred to as "the frying pan of Spain", as it features the hottest cities in the country.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-86)

Seville is the warmest city in [Continental Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Europe "Continental Europe").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-87) It is also the hottest major metropolitan area in Europe, with summer average high temperatures of above 36°C (97°F)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-88) and the hottest in Spain.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-89) After the city of [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba,_Andalusia "Córdoba, Andalusia") (also in Andalusia), Seville has the hottest summer in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") among all cities with a population over 100,000 people, with average daily highs above 36.0°C (97°F) in July and August.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-90) On average, Seville has around 60 days a year with maximum temperatures over 35.0°C (95.0°F).[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-91)

Temperatures above 40°C (104°F) are not uncommon in summer. In fact, it became the first city in the world to name a [heat wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_wave "Heat wave"), with a nickname "Zoe".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-92) The hottest temperature extreme of 46.6°C (116°F) was registered by the weather station at [Seville Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Airport "Seville Airport") on 23 July 1995 while the coldest temperature extreme of −5.5°C (22°F) was also registered by the airport weather station on 12 February 1956.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-93) A historical record high (disputed) of 50.0°C (122°F) was recorded on 4 August 1881, according to the [NOAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA "NOAA") Satellite and Information Service.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-94) There is an unaccredited record by the National Institute of Meteorology of 47.2°C (117°F) on 1 August during the [2003 heat wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_European_heat_wave "2003 European heat wave"), according to a weather station (83910 LEZL) located in the southern part of Seville Airport, near the former US San Pablo Air Force Base. This temperature would be one of the highest ever recorded in Spain, yet it has not been officially confirmed.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-95)

The average sunshine hours in Seville are approximately 3250–3300 per year. Snowfall is virtually unknown. Since the year 1500, only 10 snowfalls have been recorded/reported in Seville. During the 20th century, Seville registered just 2 snowfalls, the last one on 2 February 1954.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville#cite_note-97)

*   Winters are mild: December and January are the coolest months, with average maximum temperatures around 16 to 18°C (61 to 64°F) and minimums of 6 to 7°C (43 to 45°F).
*   Summers are very hot: July and August are the hottest months, with average maximum temperatures around 36°C (97°F) and minimums of 21°C (70°F).
*   The average yearly [precipitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precipitation_(meteorology) "Precipitation (meteorology)") is of 502 mm (19.8 in) and there are around 50 rainy days per year, with frequent [torrential rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torrential_rain "Torrential rain"). December is the wettest month, with an average rainfall around 80 millimetres (3.1 in).

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Government")]

### Municipal government and administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Municipal government and administration")]

Main article: [City Council of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Council_of_Seville "City Council of Seville")

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/15.06.13-Toma-7-_posesi%C3%B3n_Juan_Espadas_%2818154377593%29.jpg/250px-15.06.13-Toma-7-_posesi%C3%B3n_Juan_Espadas_%2818154377593%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:15.06.13-Toma-7-_posesi%C3%B3n_Juan_Espadas_(18154377593).jpg)

Plenary meeting of the municipal council in [Seville's city hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_City_Hall "Seville City Hall"), seat of _Ayuntamiento_

Seville is a [municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_of_Spain "Municipalities of Spain"), the basic level of local government in Spain. The [Ayuntamiento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayuntamiento_(Spain) "Ayuntamiento (Spain)") is the body charged with the municipal government and administration. The Plenary of the _ayuntamiento_ is formed by 31 elected municipal councillors, who in turn invest the [mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcalde "Alcalde"). The [last municipal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Seville_City_Council_election "2023 Seville City Council election") took place on 28 May 2023. The current mayor is [José Luis Sanz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Luis_Sanz "José Luis Sanz") ([People's Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Party_(Spain) "People's Party (Spain)")), who has held the post since 17 June 2023.

### Regional and provincial capital

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seville&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Regional and provincial capital")]

Seville is the capital of the autonomous community of [Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusia "Andalusia"), according to Article 4 of the [Statute of Autonomy of Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Autonomy_of_Andalusia "Statute of Autonomy of Andalusia") of 2007, and is the capital of the [Province of Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Seville "Province of Seville") as well. The historical building of the [Palace of San Telmo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_San_Telmo "Palace of San Telmo") is now the seat of the presidency of the [Andalusian Autonomous Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusian_Autonomous_Government "Andalusian Autonomous Government"). The administrative headquarters are in [Torre Triana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre_Triana "Torre Triana"), in [La Cartuja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Cartuja,_Seville "La Cartuja, Seville"). The [Hospital de las Cinco Llagas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_de_las_Cinco_Llagas "Hospital de las Cinco Llagas") (literally, "Hospital of the Five Holy Wounds") is the current seat of the [Parliament of Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Andalusia "Parliament of Andalusia").
