**Lisbon** ([/ˈ l ɪ z b ən/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/5/5d/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Vealhurl-Lisbon.wav/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Vealhurl-Lisbon.wav.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Vealhurl-Lisbon.wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Vealhurl-Lisbon.wav")[_LIZ-bən_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Lisboa_[[liʒˈβoɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Portuguese "Help:IPA/Portuguese")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/d4/Pt-pt_Lisboa_FF.ogg/Pt-pt_Lisboa_FF.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pt-pt_Lisboa_FF.ogg "File:Pt-pt Lisboa FF.ogg"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-3) is the capital and [most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Portugal "List of cities in Portugal") of [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal"), with an estimated population of 658,236 as of 2025, within its administrative limits[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Pop24-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-dgt-4) and 3,353,000 within the [metropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Metropolitan_Area "Lisbon Metropolitan Area"), as of 2025.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Pop24-1) The city lies on the Atlantic Ocean in the western part of the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula"), fronting the northern shore of the River [Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus "Tagus").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Judd2015-5) The western portion of its metro area, the [Portuguese Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Riviera "Portuguese Riviera"), hosts the westernmost point of [Continental Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Europe "Continental Europe"), culminating at [Cabo da Roca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabo_da_Roca "Cabo da Roca").

Lisbon is one of the [oldest cities in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_oldest_continuously_inhabited_cities "List of oldest continuously inhabited cities")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-RudlinThompsonJarvis2016-6) and the second-oldest European capital city (after [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens")), predating other modern European capitals by centuries.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-CIAFactbook2021-7) Settled by pre-Celtic tribes and later founded and civilised by the Phoenicians, [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar "Julius Caesar") made it a [municipium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipium "Municipium") called _Felicitas Julia_,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Livermore1973-8) adding the term to the name _[Olisipo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olisipo "Olisipo")_. After the [fall of the Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire "Fall of the Western Roman Empire"), it was ruled by a series of [Germanic tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_peoples "Germanic peoples") from the 5th century, most notably the [Visigoths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigoths "Visigoths"). Later it was captured by the [Moors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moors "Moors") in the 8th century. In 1147, [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques")[conquered the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon "Siege of Lisbon") and in 1255, it became [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal")'s capital, replacing [Coimbra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coimbra "Coimbra").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-9) It has since been the political, economic, and cultural centre of the country.

As the political centre of the country, Lisbon hosts the [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Portugal "Government of Portugal"), [Assembly of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_of_the_Republic_(Portugal) "Assembly of the Republic (Portugal)"), [Supreme Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Justice_(Portugal) "Supreme Court of Justice (Portugal)"), [Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Armed_Forces "Portuguese Armed Forces") and residence of the [head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Portugal "President of Portugal"). It is also the centre of Portuguese diplomacy, with [ambassadors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador "Ambassador") from 86 countries residing in the city, as well as representations from [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") and [Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine "Palestine").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-10) About 3.35 million people live in the [Lisbon metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_metropolitan_area "Lisbon metropolitan area"), which extends beyond the city's administrative area, making it the third largest metropolitan area in the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula") (after [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid") and [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona")) as well as figuring amongst the [10 most populous urban areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_urban_areas_in_the_European_Union "List of urban areas in the European Union") in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Statistics_Portugal_-_Web_Portal-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-World_Urban_Areas-12) It represents approximately 28% of the country's population.

Lisbon is recognised as an [alpha− level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network "Globalization and World Cities Research Network")[global city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_city "Global city") because of its importance in finance, commerce, fashion, media, entertainment, arts, international trade, education, and tourism.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-GAWC-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-14) Lisbon is amongst the two Portuguese cities (the other being [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto "Porto")) to be recognised as a global city, and it is also home to three companies in the [Global 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes_Global_2000 "Forbes Global 2000") ([EDP Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EDP_Group "EDP Group"), [Galp Energia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galp_Energia "Galp Energia") and [Jerónimo Martins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimo_Martins "Jerónimo Martins")).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-GAWC-13)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-16) Lisbon is one of the major economic centres in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"), with a growing financial sector, with [PSI-20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euronext_Lisbon "Euronext Lisbon") being part of [Euronext](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euronext "Euronext"), the largest centre for debt and funds listings in the world. The [Lisbon region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_region "Lisbon region") has a [higher GDP PPP per capita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_the_European_Union#Richest_&_Poorest_NUTS_Regions_(GDP_PPP_2007) "Economy of the European Union") than any other [region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NUTS_II "NUTS II") in Portugal, US$179 billion or $61,713 per capita. The city is the 40th richest city in the world by gross earnings.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-17) Most of the headquarters of [multinational corporations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation") in Portugal are located in the Lisbon area.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-18)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The precise origin of the name is unknown. Lisbon's name may derive from [Proto-Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Celtic "Proto-Celtic") or [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_languages "Celtic languages")_[Olisippo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olisippo "Olisippo")_, _Lissoppo_, or a similar name which other visiting ancient peoples such as the Phoenicians, Greeks, and Romans adapted accordingly, such as the pre-Roman appellation for the Tagus River, _Lisso_ or _Lucio_. Classical authors writing in Latin and Greek, including [Strabo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strabo "Strabo"), [Solinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Julius_Solinus "Gaius Julius Solinus"), and [Martianus Capella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martianus_Capella "Martianus Capella"),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-BostockRiley2015-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-StahlBurge1992-20) referred to popular legends that the city of Lisbon was founded by the mythical hero Ulysses ([Odysseus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus")).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-DelmasPenn2012-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Barletta2010-22) Lisbon's name was written _Ulyssippo_ in Latin by the geographer [Pomponius Mela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomponius_Mela "Pomponius Mela"), a native of [Hispania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania "Hispania"). It was later referred to as "Olisippo" by [Pliny the Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder "Pliny the Elder") and by the Greeks as _Olissipo_ (Ὀλισσιπών) or _Olissipona_ (Ὀλισσιπόνα).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Almeida1992-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-24)

Another claim repeated in historical literature is that the name of Lisbon could originate from a supposed ancient Phoenician term _Alis-Ubbo_, meaning "safe harbour" or "pleasant haven".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-History1780-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-FerreiraCabello1998-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Jack2019-27) Although modern archaeological excavations show there may have been Phoenician presence at this location since 1000 BC,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Whitfield2005-28) this folk etymology completely lacks any evidence and "is never attested in ancient classical literature".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Burstein2019-29)

Lisbon's name is commonly abbreviated as "LX" or "Lx", originating in an antiquated spelling of Lisbon as _Lixbõa_.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-30) While the old spelling has since been completely dropped from usage and goes against modern language standards, the abbreviation is still commonly used.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lisbon "History of Lisbon")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Lisbon "Timeline of Lisbon").

### Origins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Origins")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Escava%C3%A7%C3%B5es_no_Claustro_da_S%C3%A9_de_Lisboa.jpg/250px-Escava%C3%A7%C3%B5es_no_Claustro_da_S%C3%A9_de_Lisboa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Escava%C3%A7%C3%B5es_no_Claustro_da_S%C3%A9_de_Lisboa.jpg)

Phoenician archaeological dig in a cloister of the [Lisbon Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Cathedral "Lisbon Cathedral")

During the [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") period, the region was inhabited by Pre-Celtic tribes, who built religious and funerary monuments, [megaliths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalith "Megalith"), [dolmens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolmen "Dolmen") and [menhirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menhir "Menhir"), which still survive in areas on the periphery of Lisbon.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-31) The [Indo-European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-European_languages "Indo-European languages")[Celts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celt "Celt") invaded in the 1st millennium BC, mixing with the [Pre-Indo-European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Roman_peoples_of_the_Iberian_Peninsula "Pre-Roman peoples of the Iberian Peninsula") population, thus giving rise to Celtic-speaking local tribes such as the Cempsi or [Sefes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sefes "Sefes").

Although the first fortifications on Lisbon's [Castelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castelo_de_S%C3%A3o_Jorge "Castelo de São Jorge") hill are known to be no older than the 2nd century BC, recent archaeological finds have shown that [Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age "Iron Age") people occupied the site from the 8th to 6th centuries BC.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Bellard2003-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Arruda2002-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Laidlar1997-34) This indigenous settlement maintained commercial relations with the [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia "Phoenicia"), which would account for the recent findings of Phoenician pottery and other material objects. Archaeological excavations made near the [Castle of São Jorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle "São Jorge Castle") (_Castelo de São Jorge_) and [Lisbon Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Cathedral "Lisbon Cathedral") indicate there may have been a Phoenician presence at this location since 1000 BC,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Whitfield2005-28) and it can be stated with confidence that a Phoenician trading post stood on a site[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Pilkington2013-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-WrightSwift1971-36) now the centre of the present city, on the southern slope of the Castle hill.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-37) The sheltered harbour in the [Tagus River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus_River "Tagus River")[estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estuary "Estuary") was an ideal spot for an [Iberian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula") settlement and would have provided a secure harbour for unloading and provisioning trading ships.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-PereiraMata2012-38) The Tagus settlement was an important centre of commercial trade with the inland tribes, providing an outlet for the valuable metals, salt and salted-fish they collected, and for the sale of the [Lusitanian horses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusitano "Lusitano") renowned in antiquity.

According to a persistent legend, the location was named for the [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece") mythical king of Ithaca, [Ulysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus"), who founded the city when he sailed westward to the ends of the known world.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Jack2019-27)

### Roman era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Roman era")]

Main article: [Olisipo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olisipo "Olisipo")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/CercaMouraTorreAlfama_%28cropped%29.JPG/250px-CercaMouraTorreAlfama_%28cropped%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CercaMouraTorreAlfama_(cropped).JPG)

Part of the _Cerca Velha_ (Old Wall), originally built by the Romans[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-39)

Following the defeat of [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal") in 202 BC during the [Punic wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_wars "Punic wars"), the Romans determined to deprive [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage") of its most valuable possession: [Hispania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania "Hispania") (the Iberian Peninsula). The defeat of Carthaginian forces by [Scipio Africanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus") in Eastern Hispania allowed the pacification of the west, led by Consul [Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimus_Junius_Brutus_Callaicus "Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus"). Decimus obtained the alliance of [Olisipo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olisipo "Olisipo") (which sent men to fight alongside the Roman Legions against the northwestern Celtic tribes) by integrating it into the empire, as the _Municipium Cives Romanorum Felicitas Julia_. Local authorities were granted self-rule over a territory that extended 50 km (31 mi); exempt from taxes, its citizens were given the privileges of Roman citizenship,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Livermore1973-8) and it was then integrated with the Roman province of [Lusitania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusitania "Lusitania") (whose capital was [Emerita Augusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerita_Augusta "Emerita Augusta")).

[Lusitanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusitanians "Lusitanians") raids and rebellions during Roman occupation required the construction of a wall around the settlement. During [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus "Augustus")' reign, the Romans also built a great theatre; the Cassian Baths (underneath _Rua da Prata_); temples to [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_(mythology) "Jupiter (mythology)"), [Diana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_(mythology) "Diana (mythology)"), [Cybele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cybele "Cybele"), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(mythology) "Tethys (mythology)") and Idea [Phrygiae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrygia "Phrygia") (an uncommon cult from [Asia Minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia_Minor "Asia Minor")), in addition to temples to the Emperor; a large [necropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necropolis "Necropolis") under _[Praça da Figueira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pra%C3%A7a\_da\_Figueira "Praça da Figueira")_; a large forum and other buildings such as [insulae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insula_(building) "Insula (building)") (multi-storied apartment buildings) in the area between Castle Hill and the historic city core. Many of these ruins were first unearthed during the mid-18th century (when the recent discovery of [Pompeii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeii "Pompeii") made Roman archaeology fashionable among Europe's upper classes).

The city prospered as [piracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy "Piracy") was eliminated and technological advances were introduced, consequently _Felicitas Julia_ became a centre of trade with the Roman provinces of [Britannia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Britain "Roman Britain") (particularly [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall "Cornwall")) and the [Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine "Rhine"). Economically strong, Olisipo was known for its [garum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garum "Garum") (a fish sauce highly prized by the elites of the empire and exported in [amphorae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphora "Amphora") to Rome), wine, salt, and horse-breeding, while Roman culture permeated the hinterland. The city was connected by a broad road to Western Hispania's two other large cities, [Bracara Augusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracara_Augusta "Bracara Augusta") in the province of [Tarraconensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarraconensis "Tarraconensis") (Portuguese [Braga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braga "Braga")), and [Emerita Augusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerita_Augusta "Emerita Augusta"), the capital of [Lusitania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusitania "Lusitania"). The city was ruled by an [oligarchical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oligarchy "Oligarchy") council dominated by two families, the Julii and the Cassiae, although regional authority was administered by the Roman Governor of Emerita or directly by Emperor [Tiberius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius "Tiberius"). Among the majority of [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") speakers lived a large minority of Greek traders and slaves.

Olisipo, like most great cities in the Western Empire, was a centre for the dissemination of Christianity. Its first attested [Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriarch_of_Lisbon "Patriarch of Lisbon") was Potamius (c. 356), and there were several [martyrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martyr "Martyr") during the period of persecution of the Christians: [Verissimus, Maxima, and Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Martyrs_of_Lisbon "Holy Martyrs of Lisbon") are the most significant examples. By the time of the [Fall of Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Rome "Fall of Rome"), Olisipo had become a notable Christian centre.

[São Jorge Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_Castle "São Jorge Castle") and the surrounding neighbourhoods of [Castelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castelo_(Lisbon) "Castelo (Lisbon)"), Mouraria, and [Alfama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfama "Alfama")

### Middle Ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Middle Ages")]

Following the disintegration of the Western Roman Empire, there were [barbarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbarian "Barbarian") invasions; between 409 and 429 the city was occupied successively by [Sarmatians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarmatian "Sarmatian"), [Alans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alans "Alans") and [Vandals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandals "Vandals"). The Germanic [Suebi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suebi "Suebi"), who established a kingdom in [Gallaecia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallaecia "Gallaecia") (modern [Galicia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galicia_(Spain) "Galicia (Spain)") and northern Portugal), with its capital in _[Bracara Augusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracara\_Augusta "Bracara Augusta")_, also controlled the region of Lisbon until 585. In 585, the Suebi Kingdom was integrated into the Germanic [Visigothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigoths "Visigoths") Kingdom of Toledo, which comprised all of the Iberian Peninsula: Lisbon was then called _Ulishbona_.

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Siege_of_Lisbon_-_Muslim_surrender.jpg/250px-Siege_of_Lisbon_-_Muslim_surrender.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Siege_of_Lisbon_-_Muslim_surrender.jpg)

King [Afonso Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_Henriques "Afonso Henriques") reconquered the city from the [Almoravid Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravid_dynasty "Almoravid dynasty") at the 1147 [siege of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon "Siege of Lisbon").

On 6 August 711, Lisbon was taken by the [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moors "Moors") forces of the [Umayyad Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate "Umayyad Caliphate"). These conquerors built many mosques and houses, rebuilt the city wall (known as the _Cerca Moura_) and established administrative control, while permitting the diverse population of [Muwallads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muwallad "Muwallad"), [Arabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs"), [Berbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbers "Berbers"), [Mozarabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozarabs "Mozarabs"), _[Saqaliba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saqaliba "Saqaliba")_, and [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews") to maintain their socio-cultural lifestyles. [Mozarabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusi_Romance "Andalusi Romance") was the native language spoken by most of the Christian population although Arabic was widely known as spoken by all religious communities. Islam was the official religion practised by the Arabs, Berbers, Saqaliba and Muwallad.

The ancient Muslim influence is still visible in the [Alfama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfama "Alfama") district, an old quarter of Lisbon that survived the [1755 Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake"): many place-names are derived from Arabic and the Alfama (the oldest existing district of Lisbon) was derived from the Arabic "_al-hamma_".

For a brief time, Lisbon was an independent Muslim kingdom known as the [Taifa of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Lisbon "Taifa of Lisbon") (1022–1034), before being conquered by the larger [Taifa of Badajoz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa_of_Badajoz "Taifa of Badajoz").

In 1108 Lisbon was raided and occupied by [Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway") crusaders led by [Sigurd I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigurd_I_of_Norway "Sigurd I of Norway") on their way to the [Holy Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Land "Holy Land") as part of the [Norwegian Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Crusade "Norwegian Crusade") and occupied by crusader forces for three years.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-40) It was taken by the Moorish [Almoravids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravids "Almoravids") in 1111.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Siege_of_Lisbon_1384.JPG/250px-Siege_of_Lisbon_1384.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Siege_of_Lisbon_1384.JPG)

The [1384 siege of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon_(1384) "Siege of Lisbon (1384)") in [Froissart's Chronicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Froissart's_Chronicles "Froissart's Chronicles")

In 1147, as part of [Portuguese theatre of the Reconquista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_in_the_Reconquista "Portugal in the Reconquista"), [Afonso I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_I_of_Portugal "Afonso I of Portugal") laid [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lisbon "Siege of Lisbon") and conquered Lisbon with the aid of crusader knights. The city, with about 154,000 residents at the time, was returned to Christian rule. The conquest of Portugal and re-establishment of [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") is one of the most significant events in Lisbon's history, described in the chronicle _[Expugnatione Lyxbonensi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expugnatione\_Lyxbonensi "Expugnatione Lyxbonensi")_, which describes, among other incidents, how the local bishop was killed by the crusaders and the city's residents prayed to the [Virgin Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Mary "Virgin Mary") as it happened. Some of the Muslim residents converted to Roman Catholicism and most of those who did not convert fled to other parts of the Islamic world, primarily [Muslim Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Spain "Muslim Spain") and [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa"). All mosques were either destroyed or altered and converted into churches. As a result of the end of Muslim rule in the mid-12th century, spoken Arabic quickly lost its place in Lisbon, and disappeared altogether.

With its central location, Lisbon became the capital city of the new Portuguese territory in 1255. The first Portuguese university was founded in Lisbon in 1290 by King [Denis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinis_I_of_Portugal "Dinis I of Portugal"); for many years the _[Studium Generale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studium\_Generale "Studium Generale")_ (_General Study_) was transferred intermittently to [Coimbra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coimbra "Coimbra"), where it was installed permanently in the 16th century as the [University of Coimbra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Coimbra "University of Coimbra").

In 1384, the city was besieged by King [Juan I of Castille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_I_of_Castille "Juan I of Castille"), as a part of the ongoing [1383–1385 Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1383%E2%80%931385_Crisis "1383–1385 Crisis"). The result of the siege was a victory for the Portuguese led by [Nuno Álvares Pereira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuno_%C3%81lvares_Pereira "Nuno Álvares Pereira").

During the last centuries of the Middle Ages, Lisbon expanded substantially and became an important trading post with both [Northern European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Europe "Northern Europe") and Mediterranean cities.

### Early Modern

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Early Modern")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Lisboa_1500-1510.jpg/250px-Lisboa_1500-1510.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisboa_1500-1510.jpg)

The oldest known panorama of Lisbon (1500–1510) from the _Crónica de Dom Afonso Henriques_ by [Duarte Galvão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duarte_Galv%C3%A3o "Duarte Galvão")

When the Spaniards expelled the Jews from Spanish territory, many of them fled to Lisbon. Although acknowledging the central importance of the Jews to the city's prosperity, [Manuel I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_I_of_Portugal "Manuel I of Portugal") decreed in 1497 that all Jews must convert to Christianity, only those who refused being forced to leave, but not before the expropriation of their property.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Roitman2011-41) In 1506, a [four-day anti-Semitic riot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_massacre "Lisbon massacre") by [Old Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Christians "Old Christians") in Lisbon led to the deaths of about 1,000 to 4,000 "[New Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Christians "New Christians")", the descendants of [Sephardic Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardic_Jews "Sephardic Jews") whom were primarily forced to convert.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Soyer2007-42) The king was at Évora when these events occurred, but angered when he received the news, he ordered an investigation which resulted in two of the instigating friars being excommunicated and burned alive.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-PintoMateus2014-43)

Most of the Portuguese expeditions of the [Age of Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery "Age of Discovery") set out from Lisbon during the period from the end of the 15th century to the beginning of the 17th century, including [Vasco da Gama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama "Vasco da Gama")'s expedition to [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") in 1498. The following years of the 16th century began Lisbon's golden era: the city was the European hub of commerce between [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Portugal_(1415%E2%80%931578) "History of Portugal (1415–1578)"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_India "Portuguese India"), the [Far East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanban_trade "Nanban trade") and later, [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Brazil "Colonial Brazil"), and acquired great riches by exploiting the trade in spices, slaves, sugar, textiles and other goods. This period saw the rise of the exuberant [Manueline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manueline "Manueline") style in architecture, which left its mark in many 16th-century monuments (including Lisbon's [Belém Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower "Belém Tower") and [Jerónimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery"), which were declared [UNESCO World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO_World_Heritage_Sites "UNESCO World Heritage Sites")). A description of Lisbon in the 16th century was written by [Damião de Góis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A3o_de_G%C3%B3is "Damião de Góis") and published in 1554.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-44)

Panoramic drawing of Lisbon done by Pier Maria Baldi in 1669, who accompanied Cosme III de Médici in his european travels. Both the Corte Real Palace (on the left by the riverside), the Ribeira Palace (in the middle), the Sé of Lisbon and Saint George's Castle can be seen.

The [succession crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Union "Iberian Union") of 1580 initiated a sixty-year period of dual monarchy in Portugal and Spain under the [Spanish Habsburgs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_Spain "Habsburg Spain").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-46) This is referred to as the "Philippine Dominion" (_Domínio Filipino_), since all [three Spanish kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Dynasty "Philippine Dynasty") during that period were called Philip (_Filipe_). In 1589, Lisbon was the target of an incursion by the [English Armada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Armada "English Armada") led by [Francis Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Drake "Francis Drake"), while [Queen Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I "Elizabeth I") supported a Portuguese [pretender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretender "Pretender") in [Antonio, Prior of Crato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio,_Prior_of_Crato "Antonio, Prior of Crato"), but support for Crato was lacking and the expedition was a failure. The [Portuguese Restoration War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Restoration_War "Portuguese Restoration War"), which began with a [coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d'%C3%A9tat "Coup d'état") organised by the nobility and [bourgeoisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeois "Bourgeois") in Lisbon and executed on 1 December 1640, restored Portuguese independence. The period from 1640 to 1668 was marked by periodic skirmishes between Portugal and Spain, as well as short episodes of more serious warfare until the [Treaty of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lisbon_(1668) "Treaty of Lisbon (1668)") was signed in 1668.

In the early 18th century, gold from Brazil allowed [King John V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V_of_Portugal "John V of Portugal") to sponsor the building of several [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque "Baroque") churches and theatres in the city. Prior to the 18th century, Lisbon had experienced several significant earthquakes – eight in the 14th century, five in the 16th century (including the [1531 earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1531_Lisbon_earthquake "1531 Lisbon earthquake") that destroyed 1,500 houses and the 1597 earthquake in which three streets vanished), and three in the 17th century.

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Vista_dos_Jeronomis_por_Filipe_Lobo_%282%29.jpg/250px-Vista_dos_Jeronomis_por_Filipe_Lobo_%282%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vista_dos_Jeronomis_por_Filipe_Lobo_(2).jpg)

[King Manuel I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_I_of_Portugal "Manuel I of Portugal") ordered [Jerónimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery") to be built in [Belém](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_(Lisbon) "Belém (Lisbon)"), to serve [Portuguese discoverers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_discoveries "Portuguese discoveries").

On 1 November 1755, the city was destroyed by another [devastating earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake"), which killed an estimated 30,000 to 40,000 Lisbon residents[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Pereira2006-47) of a population estimated at between 200,000 and 275,000,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-Pereira2006-47):8[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-NISEE1755-48) and destroyed 85 percent of the city's structures.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-NISEE1755-48) Among several important buildings of the city, the [Ribeira Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribeira_Palace "Ribeira Palace") and the [Hospital Real de Todos os Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_Real_de_Todos_os_Santos "Hospital Real de Todos os Santos") were lost. In coastal areas, such as [Peniche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peniche_Municipality "Peniche Municipality"), situated about 80 kilometres (50 mi) north of Lisbon, many people were killed by the following [tsunami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami "Tsunami").

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Ruinas_da_Pra%C3%A7a_da_Patriarcal_ap%C3%B3s_o_Terramoto_de_1755_-_Jacques_Philippe_Le_Bas%2C_1757.png/250px-Ruinas_da_Pra%C3%A7a_da_Patriarcal_ap%C3%B3s_o_Terramoto_de_1755_-_Jacques_Philippe_Le_Bas%2C_1757.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ruinas_da_Pra%C3%A7a_da_Patriarcal_ap%C3%B3s_o_Terramoto_de_1755_-_Jacques_Philippe_Le_Bas,_1757.png)

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Ruinas_da_Igreja_de_S._Nicolau_ap%C3%B3s_o_Terramoto_de_1755_-_Jacques_Philippe_Le_Bas%2C_1757.png/250px-Ruinas_da_Igreja_de_S._Nicolau_ap%C3%B3s_o_Terramoto_de_1755_-_Jacques_Philippe_Le_Bas%2C_1757.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ruinas_da_Igreja_de_S._Nicolau_ap%C3%B3s_o_Terramoto_de_1755_-_Jacques_Philippe_Le_Bas,_1757.png)

The [1755 Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake") devastated Lisbon with an estimated magnitude between 8.5 and 9.0.

By 1755, Lisbon was one of the largest cities in Europe; the catastrophic event shocked the whole of Europe and left a deep impression on its collective psyche. [Voltaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire "Voltaire") wrote a long poem, _[Poème sur le désastre de Lisbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Po%C3%A8me\_sur\_le\_d%C3%A9sastre\_de\_Lisbonne "Poème sur le désastre de Lisbonne")_, shortly after the quake, and mentioned it in his 1759 novel _[Candide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candide "Candide")_ (indeed, many argue that this critique of [optimism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimism "Optimism") was inspired by that earthquake). [Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Wendell_Holmes_Sr. "Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.") also mentions it in his 1857 poem, _The Deacon's Masterpiece, or The Wonderful One-Hoss Shay_.

After the 1755 earthquake, the city was rebuilt largely according to the plans of Prime Minister [Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebasti%C3%A3o_Jos%C3%A9_de_Carvalho_e_Melo "Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo"), the [1st Marquis of Pombal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquis_of_Pombal "Marquis of Pombal"); the lower town began to be known as the _Baixa Pombalina_ ([Pombaline central district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pombaline_Lower_Town "Pombaline Lower Town")). Instead of rebuilding the medieval town, Pombal decided to demolish what remained after the earthquake and rebuild the city centre in accordance with principles of modern urban design. It was reconstructed in an open rectangular plan with two great squares: the _[Praça do Rossio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pra%C3%A7a\_do\_Rossio "Praça do Rossio")_ and the _[Praça do Comércio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pra%C3%A7a\_do\_Com%C3%A9rcio "Praça do Comércio")_. The first, the central commercial district, is the traditional gathering place of the city and the location of the older cafés, theatres and restaurants; the second became the city's main access to the River Tagus and point of departure and arrival for seagoing vessels, adorned by a triumphal arch (1873) and a monument to King [Joseph I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_I_of_Portugal "Joseph I of Portugal").

### Modern era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Modern era")]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Lisbon%2C_the_Pal%C3%A1cio_Nacional_da_Ajuda.JPG/250px-Lisbon%2C_the_Pal%C3%A1cio_Nacional_da_Ajuda.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon,_the_Pal%C3%A1cio_Nacional_da_Ajuda.JPG)

The [Palace of Ajuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Ajuda "Palace of Ajuda") was built as a residence for the [King of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Portugal "King of Portugal") following the [1755 Lisbon Earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_Earthquake "1755 Lisbon Earthquake").

In the first years of the 19th century, Portugal was invaded by the troops of [Napoléon Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napol%C3%A9on_Bonaparte "Napoléon Bonaparte"), forcing Queen [Maria I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_I_of_Portugal "Maria I of Portugal") and Prince-Regent [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_VI_of_Portugal "John VI of Portugal") (future John VI) to flee temporarily to Brazil. The capital of the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves was located in Rio de Janeiro from 1808 to 1821. By the time the new King returned to Lisbon, many of the buildings and properties were pillaged, sacked or destroyed by the invaders.

During the 19th century, the Liberal movement introduced new changes into the urban landscape. The principal areas were in the _Baixa_ and along the _Chiado_ district, where shops, tobacconists shops, cafés, bookstores, clubs and theatres proliferated. The development of industry and commerce determined the growth of the city, seeing the transformation of the [Passeio Público](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passeio_P%C3%BAblico_(Lisbon) "Passeio Público (Lisbon)"), a Pombaline era park, into the [Avenida da Liberdade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenida_da_Liberdade "Avenida da Liberdade"), as the city grew farther from the Tagus.

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Proclama%C3%A7%C3%A3o_Rep%C3%BAblica_Portuguesa.jpg/250px-Proclama%C3%A7%C3%A3o_Rep%C3%BAblica_Portuguesa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Proclama%C3%A7%C3%A3o_Rep%C3%BAblica_Portuguesa.jpg)

The [Proclamation of the Portuguese Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5_October_1910_revolution "5 October 1910 revolution") in 1910

Lisbon was the site of the [regicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Regicide "Lisbon Regicide") of [Carlos I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_I_of_Portugal "Carlos I of Portugal") in 1908, an event which culminated two years later with the [5 October 1910 revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5_October_1910_revolution "5 October 1910 revolution"), brought an end to the [Portuguese monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_monarchy "Portuguese monarchy") and established the highly unstable and corrupt [Portuguese First Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_First_Republic "Portuguese First Republic").

The city refounded its university in 1911 after centuries of inactivity in Lisbon, incorporating reformed former colleges and other non-university higher education schools of the city (such as the _Escola Politécnica_, now _Faculdade de Ciências_). Today, there are two public universities in the city ([University of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Lisbon "University of Lisbon") and [New University of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_University_of_Lisbon "New University of Lisbon")), a public university institute ([ISCTE - Lisbon University Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISCTE_-_Lisbon_University_Institute "ISCTE - Lisbon University Institute")) and a [polytechnic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytechnic_(Portugal) "Polytechnic (Portugal)") institute (IPL – [Instituto Politécnico de Lisboa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_Polit%C3%A9cnico_de_Lisboa "Instituto Politécnico de Lisboa")).

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/33286-Padr%C3%A3o_dos_Descobrimentos_%2836569390292%29.jpg/250px-33286-Padr%C3%A3o_dos_Descobrimentos_%2836569390292%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:33286-Padr%C3%A3o_dos_Descobrimentos_(36569390292).jpg)

[Monument of the Discoveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_of_the_Discoveries "Monument of the Discoveries") was built for the [1940 Portuguese World Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_World_Exhibition "Portuguese World Exhibition").

The city was also the site where the [28 May 1926 coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/28_May_1926_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "28 May 1926 coup d'état") ended the first republic and firmly established the [Estado Novo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estado_Novo_(Portugal) "Estado Novo (Portugal)"), or the [Portuguese Second Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Second_Republic "Portuguese Second Republic"), as the ruling regime. During the Estado Novo regime (1926–1974), Lisbon, under the influence of [Duarte Pacheco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duarte_Pacheco "Duarte Pacheco"), the minister of works, was expanded at the cost of other districts within the country, resulting in nationalist and monumental projects.

New residential and public developments were constructed; the zone of [Belém](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_(Lisbon) "Belém (Lisbon)") was modified for the [1940 Portuguese Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_World_Exhibition "Portuguese World Exhibition"), while along the periphery new districts appeared to house the growing population. The inauguration of the bridge over the Tagus allowed a rapid connection between both sides of the river.

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_in_World_War_II "Portugal in World War II"), Lisbon was one of the very few neutral, open European Atlantic ports, a major gateway for refugees to the U.S. and a haven for spies. More than 100,000 refugees were able to flee [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") via Lisbon.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-49)

### Contemporary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Contemporary")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Parque_das_Na%C3%A7%C3%B5es_-_Lisboa_%28Portugal%29.jpg/250px-Parque_das_Na%C3%A7%C3%B5es_-_Lisboa_%28Portugal%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Parque_das_Na%C3%A7%C3%B5es_-_Lisboa_(Portugal).jpg)

Lisbon's [Expo '98](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expo_'98 "Expo '98") mascot, "Gil".

The [Carnation Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnation_Revolution "Carnation Revolution"), which took place on 25 April 1974, ended the right-wing [Estado Novo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estado_Novo_(Portugal) "Estado Novo (Portugal)") regime and reformed the country to its current state as the [Portuguese Third Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Third_Republic "Portuguese Third Republic").

In the 1990s, many of the districts were renovated and projects in the historic quarters were established to modernise those areas. Architectural and patrimonial buildings were renovated, the northern margin of the Tagus was re-purposed for leisure and residential use, the [Vasco da Gama Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Bridge "Vasco da Gama Bridge") was constructed and the eastern part of the municipality was re-purposed for [Expo '98](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expo_'98 "Expo '98") to commemorate the 500th anniversary of [Vasco da Gama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama "Vasco da Gama")'s sea voyage to India, which brought immense riches to Lisbon and led to the construction of many of Lisbon's landmarks.

In 1988, a fire in the historical district of [Chiado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiado "Chiado") saw the destruction of many 18th-century [Pombaline style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pombaline_style "Pombaline style") buildings. A series of restoration works has brought the area back to its former self and made it a high-scale shopping district.

The [Lisbon Agenda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Agenda "Lisbon Agenda") was a European Union agreement on measures to revitalise the EU economy, signed in Lisbon in March 2000. In October 2007 Lisbon hosted the [2007 EU Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_EU_Summit "2007 EU Summit"), where an agreement was reached regarding a new EU governance model. The resulting [Treaty of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lisbon "Treaty of Lisbon") was signed on 13 December 2007 and came into force on 1 December 2009.

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Tratado_de_Lisboa_13_12_2007_%2808%29_edited.jpg/250px-Tratado_de_Lisboa_13_12_2007_%2808%29_edited.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tratado_de_Lisboa_13_12_2007_(08)_edited.jpg)

The [Treaty of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lisbon "Treaty of Lisbon"), which forms the constitutional basis of the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"), was signed at the [Jerónimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery") in 2007.

Lisbon has been the site for many international events and programmes. In 1994, Lisbon was the [European Capital of Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Capital_of_Culture "European Capital of Culture"). On 3 November 2005, Lisbon hosted the [MTV European Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Europe_Music_Awards_2005 "MTV Europe Music Awards 2005"). On 7 July 2007, Lisbon held the ceremony of the "New 7 Wonders Of The World"[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-50) election, in the [Luz Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Est%C3%A1dio_da_Luz "Estádio da Luz"), with live transmission for millions of people all over the world. Every two years, Lisbon hosts the [Rock in Rio Lisboa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_in_Rio#Lisboa,_Portugal,_and_Madrid,_Spain "Rock in Rio") Music Festival, one of the largest in the world. Lisbon hosted the [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") summit (19–20 November 2010), a [summit meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_(meeting) "Summit (meeting)") that is regarded as a periodic opportunity for Heads of State and [Heads of Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_Government "Head of Government") of [NATO member states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_member_states "NATO member states") to evaluate and provide strategic direction for Alliance activities.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-51) The city hosts the [Web Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_Summit "Web Summit") and is the head office for the [Group of Seven Plus (G7+)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7+ "G7+"). In 2018 it hosted the [Eurovision Song Contest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest_2018 "Eurovision Song Contest 2018") for the first time as well as the [Michelin Gala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelin_Guide "Michelin Guide").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-52) On 11 July 2018, the [Aga Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aga_Khan_IV "Aga Khan IV") officially chose the Henrique de Mendonça Palace, located on Rua Marquês de Fronteira, as the _[Divan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divan "Divan")_, or seat, of the global [Nizari Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nizari_Isma'ilism "Nizari Isma'ilism")[Imamate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imamate "Imamate").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-54) Lisbon hosted [World Youth Day 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Youth_Day_2023 "World Youth Day 2023") in August of that year, attracting [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholicism "Catholicism") youth from the around the world. [Pope Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Francis "Pope Francis") led several events, with the final [mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_(liturgy) "Mass (liturgy)") held in the city's Parque do Tejo having an estimated 1.5 million attendees.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-57)

### Physical geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Physical geography")]

Lisbon is located at [38°42′49.75″N 9°8′21.79″W / 38.7138194°N 9.1393861°W / 38.7138194; -9.1393861](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Lisbon&params=38_42_49.75_N_9_8_21.79_W_type:city(2042326)_region:PT), situated at the mouth of the [Tagus River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus_River "Tagus River") and is the westernmost capital of a mainland European country. The river delta is [inverted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverted_river_delta "Inverted river delta").

The westernmost part of Lisbon is occupied by the [Monsanto Forest Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsanto_Forest_Park "Monsanto Forest Park"), a ten-square-kilometre urban park, one of the largest in Europe, which takes up 10% of the municipality.

The city occupies an area of 100.05 square kilometres (38.63 square miles); its city boundaries, unlike those of most major cities, coincide with those of the municipality.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-58) The rest of the urbanised area of the Lisbon urban area, known generically as [Greater Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grande_Lisboa_Subregion "Grande Lisboa Subregion") ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Grande Lisboa_) includes several administratively defined cities and municipalities, in the north bank of the Tagus River. The larger [Lisbon metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_metropolitan_area "Lisbon metropolitan area") includes the [Setúbal Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pen%C3%ADnsula_de_Set%C3%BAbal "Península de Setúbal") to the south.

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lisbon&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Climate")]

Main article: [Climate of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Lisbon "Climate of Lisbon")

Lisbon has a [Mediterranean climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_climate "Mediterranean climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): _Csa_),[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-59) characterised by mild, rainy winters and warm to hot, dry summers. The average annual temperature is 17.6°C (63.7°F), with average daily highs of 21.7°C (71.1°F) and lows of 13.6°C (56.5°F).

In the coldest month, January, daytime highs typically range from 14 to 19°C (57 to 66°F), while nighttime lows range from 5 to 10°C (41 to 50°F), with an average sea temperature of 16°C (61°F).[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-seatemperature-60) In the warmest month, August, daytime highs typically range from 25 to 32°C (77 to 90°F), nighttime lows range from 14 to 20°C (57 to 68°F), and the average sea temperature is about 20°C (68°F).[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-seatemperature-60)

The climate of Lisbon is moderate, largely due to its location in southwestern Europe, its proximity to the [Azores High](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores_High "Azores High")[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-61) and the Atlantic Ocean. The highest temperature ever recorded in Lisbon was 44.0°C (111.2°F) on 4 August 2018,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-62) while the lowest temperature ever recorded was −1.5°C (29°F) on February 15, 1860;[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-IPMA535-63) although other locations in its [metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_metropolitan_area "Lisbon metropolitan area") have recorded lower temperatures, not being as affected by the [urban heat island effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_heat_island_effect "Urban heat island effect")[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-64) of the city centre, with [Sintra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sintra "Sintra") and [Setúbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set%C3%BAbal "Setúbal") having reached −4°C (25°F) and −5.1°C (22.8°F), respectively, both experiencing about 13 days of frost per year on average.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-66)

Lisbon receives about 793 mm (31.2 in) of precipitation annually, with the majority falling during the autumn and winter months. November and December are the wettest months, contributing to a third of the total annual rainfall. The dry season typically lasts from early June to mid-September, with July and August being the driest months. During this period, there are typically about 8 days with measurable precipitation.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-IPMA-67)

The city has about 2,875 hours of sunshine per year, one of the highest amounts in Europe. August is the sunniest month, with sunshine occurring for approximately 80% of the daytime, while December is the dullest, with sunshine occurring only 51% of the time.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon#cite_note-dwd-68)

Temperatures across Lisbon's metropolitan area can vary significantly, especially during the summer months. In areas with greater exposure to the Atlantic Ocean, such as [Sintra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sintra "Sintra") or [Cascais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascais "Cascais") to the west of the city, temperatures tend to be more moderate and are generally cooler. In extreme cases, summer daytime highs can differ by as much as 20°C (68°F) between the city of Lisbon and [Cabo da Roca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabo_da_Roca "Cabo da Roca").
